surface: ないわけにはいかない
reading: ないわけにはいかない
meanings: can't not do; have no choice but to do
structure: Verb［ない form］＋わけにはいかない
explanation: 〜ないわけにはいかない expresses obligation that comes from social or psychological pressure: given the circumstances, not doing the action is simply not an option, so you have to do it. 行かないわけにはいかない = 'I can't very well not go'. The reason is usually a duty, expectation, or relationship rather than physical necessity.

synonyms.note: ざるを得ない also means 'have no choice but to'; it is more formal and stresses external force rather than social duty.
なければならない is neutral necessity; ないわけにはいかない adds the sense of being socially or morally unable to refuse.

related.note: Positive わけにはいかない means 'cannot do (for such reasons)'; adding ない flips it to 'cannot not do'.

surface: ちゃいけない・じゃいけない
reading: ちゃいけない・じゃいけない
meanings: must not do ~ (casual)
structure: Verb［て form: ては → ちゃ］＋ いけない
Verb［て form: では → じゃ］＋ いけない
explanation: A spoken contraction of てはいけない that expresses prohibition — "you must not ~". て + は shrinks to ちゃ, and で + は (from verbs ending in で) shrinks to じゃ. Use it in casual conversation where the full form would feel stiff.

related.note: な is a blunt, direct "don't"; ちゃいけない states a rule against doing it.

meanings: there's no way ~; cannot possibly be
structure: Verb ／ い-adjective［plain form］＋ はずがない
な-adjective ＋ な ＋ はずがない
Noun ＋ の ＋ はずがない
explanation: はずがない voices the speaker's strong confidence that something is not so — 'there's no way that ~'. You reason from what you know and conclude the situation is impossible or highly unlikely. It attaches to plain forms, with な-adjective＋な and noun＋の; はずはない is a slightly softer variant.

synonyms.note: わけがない is a very close 'there's no way'; はずがない frames it as a defied expectation.

antonyms.note: はずだ expects something to be true; はずがない insists it cannot be.

meanings: to go out of one's way to; to take the trouble of doing
explanation: わざわざ is an adverb that marks an action as a special, deliberate effort — one that went beyond what was strictly needed, like making a special trip or taking extra trouble. It often acknowledges someone's kindness (thanks for going to the bother), and can also gently point out that such effort wasn't really necessary.

related.note: わざと is doing something deliberately to cause a result (often a bad one); わざわざ stresses the extra trouble taken, usually with goodwill.
〜てまで frames effort as going 'so far as to' an extreme; わざわざ simply notes that a special effort was made.

surface: たらさいご・たがさいご
reading: たらさいご・たがさいご
meanings: once you do ~, that's the end of it; there's no going back
explanation: 〜たら最後 (or the more emphatic 〜たが最後) says that once a certain action occurs, an inevitable and usually undesirable consequence follows, with no way back — 一度引き受けたら最後、途中でやめられない = once you take it on, there's no quitting halfway. Built on the た-form, it stresses a point of no return.

synonyms.note: ばそれまでだ means 'if ~, then it's all over'; たら最後 stresses that the action itself sets off an unstoppable chain.
ようものなら warns of dire consequences if one merely tried something; たら最後 says the deed, once done, cannot be undone.

related.note: ものなら sets up a hypothetical with serious consequences; たら最後 fixes on the irreversible point after the action.

meanings: whether ~ or ~; either way; to a greater or lesser degree
structure: い-adjective［classical stem］＋かれ＋（opposite）＋かれ［fixed set phrase］
explanation: かれ〜かれ pairs two opposite adjective stems in a fixed idiom meaning that whichever of the two holds, the same conclusion applies. It survives only in set phrases: 遅かれ早かれ (sooner or later), 多かれ少なかれ (more or less, to some degree), 良かれ悪しかれ (for better or worse). The かれ is a classical adjective ending, so these are memorized wholes rather than a freely built pattern.

meanings: if ~ (then); provided that ~
structure: い-adjective［ー い → ければ］
explanation: The ば conditional sets up a general 'if A, then B' link: when the condition holds, the result naturally follows. It suits natural consequences, general truths, and advice. Build it by changing a verb's final -u to -eba (押す → 押せば), an い-adjective's い to ければ (安い → 安ければ), and a noun or な-adjective with なら（ば）; the negative uses なければ.

related.note: たら fits one-time 'once A happens, B' sequences; ば states a more general condition-result rule.
と is for automatic, inevitable results; ば allows advice and commands more freely.
なら responds to a topic just raised ('if that's the case'); ば states a plain condition.

meanings: on one hand ~, on the other hand ~; while
explanation: 〜一方（で） contrasts two sides of a situation that hold at the same time — 'on one hand…, while on the other…'. 明るい一方で = cheerful, while (on the other hand)…. It links two coexisting facts that pull in different directions, often about the same person or thing.

synonyms.note: 〜反面 also contrasts two sides of the same thing; 一方で can present two separate subjects side by side as well.

related.note: 逆に flips to the opposite ('conversely'); 一方で holds up two coexisting sides at once.
一方だ uses the same 一方 but means a situation only keeps ~ing; 一方で marks a two-sided contrast.

meanings: nothing but; merely; all that remains is
explanation: ただ〜のみだ frames something as 'nothing but ~' or 'all that is left is ~'. のみ is the literary equivalent of だけ, and ただ reinforces it with the sense of 'merely / simply'. あとはただ待つのみだ = all that remains now is to wait. It attaches to a dictionary-form verb or a noun and belongs to formal, written-style Japanese.

synonyms.note: のみ alone already means 'only' in a literary register; ただ〜のみだ frames it emphatically as 'nothing but'.
だけ is the everyday word for 'only'; ただ〜のみだ is its formal, emphatic counterpart.

related.note: ばかり also limits to 'only / just', but colloquially and often with a nuance of excess; ただ〜のみだ is formal and clean.

surface: てかなわない・てはかなわない
reading: てかなわない・てはかなわない
meanings: unbearably ~; can't stand it that ~; too ~ to put up with
explanation: 〜てかなわない says a condition is more than the speaker can bear — it is unbearably or intolerably so. 暑くてかなわない = unbearably hot, this heat is too much. It typically follows adjectives or verbs describing a sensation or feeling and expresses the speaker's own discomfort. The variant 〜てはかなわない frames it as 'it would be unbearable if ~', pushing back against a possibility.

synonyms.note: 〜てたまらない ('unbearably ~') is close and a touch more neutral in feeling; てかなわない stresses annoyance and exasperation at having to put up with it.
〜てならない marks a feeling that wells up uncontrollably; てかなわない specifically marks something as too much to endure.
〜てしょうがない ('can't help feeling ~') is the casual all-purpose version; てかなわない leans toward an intolerable nuisance.

meanings: like (a noun); similar to ~
explanation: のように and のような compare something to a noun. Use のように before a verb or adjective (歌手のように歌う = sing like a singer) and のような before a noun (雪のような花 = flowers like snow). The noun before の is the thing being resembled, giving a vivid 'just like ~' comparison.

related.note: みたいに・みたいな is the casual equivalent of のように・のような after a noun.
ように・ような can follow verbs and clauses too; のように・のような attaches specifically to a noun.
ようだ is the predicate 'seems / is like' form of the same よう.

meanings: if it were ~, that'd be one thing, but ~
explanation: 〜ならともかく sets aside one case as understandable or excusable in order to contrast it with the actual case, which is not. 子供ならともかく = 'if it were a child it'd be one thing, but...'. The ならともかく clause names the acceptable hypothetical; the main clause states the real, often problematic situation, frequently with a critical tone.

synonyms.note: ならまだしも is very close ('if ~ then maybe, but'); both concede one case, with まだしも stressing 'still tolerable'.
はともかく simply sets a topic aside ('leaving ~ aside'); ならともかく contrasts a hypothetical acceptable case with the real one.

surface: ぜんしゃは・こうしゃは
reading: ぜんしゃは・こうしゃは
meanings: the former ~ ; the latter ~
explanation: 前者 means "the former" (the first of two things mentioned) and 後者 means "the latter" (the second). Used together, they let you refer back to two items without repeating them: 前者は安く、後者は速い = the former is cheap, the latter is fast. It's a formal pairing, common in writing and comparisons.

meanings: was under the impression that; had assumed that
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ものと思っていた
explanation: The past continuous 〜ものと思っていた describes an assumption the speaker held over some period — 'I was under the impression that ~'. It very often implies that the assumption later turned out to be mistaken: てっきり来るものと思っていた = I was sure he'd come (but he didn't). It attaches to a plain-form clause and is frequently paired with てっきり ('quite certainly').

synonyms.note: ものと思う is a present, still-held assumption; ものと思っていた is a past belief, often one that turned out to be wrong.

related.note: はずだった expresses 'was supposed to be' from expectation; ものと思っていた reports a mistaken impression the speaker carried.

surface: ようが〜まいが・ようと〜まいと
reading: ようが〜まいが・ようと〜まいと
meanings: whether one does or not; regardless of whether ~
structure: Verb［volitional］＋が／と＋（same verb）＋まいが／まいと
explanation: This pattern pairs a volitional (〜よう) with the negative volitional まい to mean 'whether one does ~ or not': 行こうが行くまいが = whether you go or not. The main clause holds true regardless of which side is the case. まい attaches to the dictionary form of godan verbs (行くまい) and to either form of ichidan/する verbs (食べまい／食べるまい, しまい／するまい). related.note: まい on its own is the negative volitional ('probably won't / won't'); here it forms the negative half of the 'whether or not' pair.

meanings: just like; as if; as though
structure: まるで ＋ 〜ようだ／みたいだ／のように
explanation: まるで sets up a vivid 'just like' comparison and normally finishes with ようだ／みたい／のように — まるで夢のようだ = 'It's just like a dream.' Leaving off that ending sounds incomplete. With a negative ending, まるで〜ない instead means 'not at all' (まるで違う = completely different).

related.note: ようだ ('seems like / is like') is the ending まるで usually leads into; まるで intensifies it to 'just like'.
みたい is the casual 'like'; まるで often teams with it for an emphatic 'just like'.
かのように is a more literary 'as if'; まるで is the everyday adverb that sets up the same comparison.

meanings: -ness; the quality or felt sense of ~ (turns an adjective into a noun)
explanation: 〜み attaches to an adjective stem to make a noun for the quality itself, often something you can feel or sense — 痛み = pain, 深み = depth, 温かみ = warmth. It works with a limited set of adjectives, not every one, and tends to name a felt quality rather than a measurable amount.

synonyms.note: 〜さ freely makes a degree noun from almost any adjective (高さ, 大きさ); 〜み names a felt quality and joins only certain adjectives.

related.note: 〜げ makes an adjective for how something looks or seems (寂しげ = looking lonely); 〜み makes a noun for the quality itself.
〜がり labels a person prone to a feeling (寒がり); 〜み names the quality or sensation, not a person.

meanings: be about to do; on the verge of doing
explanation: A dictionary-form verb ＋ ところだ places you right before an action starts — you are just about to do it. ところ pins down the moment on a timeline: with the dictionary form it is 'about to', contrasting with ているところ ('in the middle of') and たところ ('just finished').

related.note: ているところ is being in the middle of the action; るところ is just before it.
たところ is having just finished; るところ is about to start.

meanings: there's no chance of ~; definitely won't / can't
explanation: っこない attaches to the ます-stem to flatly deny that something could ever happen — 分かりっこない = 'there's no way I'd understand', 勝てっこない = 'we can't possibly win'. It is a casual, spoken way to voice the speaker's firm conviction that something is impossible, close in meaning to はずがない but far more colloquial.

synonyms.note: わけがない also denies possibility but is neutral in register; っこない is distinctly casual and spoken.
はずがない reasons that something 'can't be so'; っこない is a blunter, colloquial 'no way it'll happen'.

related.note: まい is a formal/written negative conjecture ('surely won't'); っこない carries the same certainty in casual speech.

meanings: do ~ (mild command from a superior to a subordinate)
explanation: たまえ attaches to the ます-stem to give a gentle order from someone of higher standing to someone below — a boss to a subordinate, a teacher to a student. It sounds masculine, somewhat old-fashioned and literary, and softer than a blunt imperative. It is rare in everyday modern speech.

synonyms.note: なさい is a firm command often used parent-to-child; たまえ is masculine, superior-to-subordinate, and more dated.

related.note: 命令形 is the blunt imperative like しろ/来い; たまえ is a gentler, more refined order.

meanings: i-adjective directly modifying a noun

meanings: depending on; in accordance with; to match ~
explanation: 〜に応じて means something varies flexibly in response to a changing condition — the result adjusts to fit it. 収入に応じて = 'according to income'. It attaches to nouns, and 〜に応じた modifies a following noun (要望に応じたプラン). The nuance is adaptation: as the condition changes, the outcome changes with it.

次第で means the outcome hinges on ~ ('depending on'); に応じて stresses proportional adjustment to the condition.

related.note: によって covers 'depending on / by means of / due to' broadly; に応じて specifically means adapting flexibly to fit.

meanings: gradually; little by little

explanation: だんだん describes a change that happens slowly and steadily over time. It sits before the verb and pairs naturally with verbs of change like 〜なる, 〜くなる, and 〜てくる／〜ていく. Reach for it when something shifts bit by bit, such as the weather warming up.

synonyms.note: 次第に is a more formal 'gradually'; だんだん is the everyday word.

related.note: どんどん is fast, vigorous 'more and more'; だんだん is slow and steady.
だんだん often teams with なる to describe a gradual change of state.

meanings: there's no need to; not a match for; falls short of
explanation: 〜には及ばない has two senses. After a dictionary-form verb it means 'there's no need to ~' — 心配するには及ばない = no need to worry. After a noun it means 'does not measure up to / is no match for' — 彼の腕には及ばない = not up to his skill. meanings: worth doing / holds up to ~ ; unbearable to ~ ; filled with (emotion)
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋に耐える／に耐えない

synonyms.note: に値する means 'is worth / deserves ~' as a positive judgment; に耐える means it is solid enough to hold up to something like appreciation.

related.note: に足りない means 'not worth ~ing / not enough to'; に耐えない means 'unbearable to ~' or 'filled with (emotion)'.
に忍びない is 'too pitiful to bear'; 見るに耐えない is 'too unpleasant to keep watching' — sympathy versus distaste.

explanation: 〜ところを marks a situation or moment and then says that, despite it, something happens — most often in set courtesy phrases thanking or apologizing for imposing at an inconvenient time. お忙しいところを = though you are busy, お休みのところを = though you were resting. meanings: as of (the end of); ~ being the last
explanation: 〜を限りに takes a time point or occasion as the final cutoff, after which something stops or changes for good: 今日を限りに = as of today; 本日を限りに閉店 = closing as of today. synonyms.note: をもって is a neutral formal 'as of / with (this)'; を限りに adds the feeling that this is the final time, the last.

related.note: を境に marks a dividing line with a before/after change; を限りに marks a final endpoint after which something simply stops.

explanation: 〜ないでもない is a double negative that expresses reluctant or partial affirmation — 'it's not that I don't ~ / I kind of do'. 気持ちは分からないでもない = I can sort of see how you feel. meanings: cannot; there is no possibility of; it is unthinkable that
explanation: 〜得ない (read えない) attaches to the ます-stem to say that something is impossible or unthinkable — あり得ない = cannot be / impossible, 考え得ない = inconceivable. variants.explanation: Talks about past experience: attach ことがある to a verb's た form to say "I have done ~ (at least once) before". Use it to share what you have or haven't tried, or to ask someone whether they have ever done something.

related.note: Dictionary form + ことがある means "there are times I do ~"; the た form means "have done before".
ことができる expresses ability ("can do"); たことがある expresses experience.

meanings: instantly; in no time; in a flash
explanation: たちまち is an adverb meaning that something happens with great speed, almost at once — a change completes 'in no time'. It often describes a sudden, sometimes striking shift affecting a whole situation, and feels more vivid and literary than すぐ.

related.note: たとたん(に) marks the exact moment one thing triggers another; たちまち describes the rapid speed of a change.

meanings: from the fact that; judging from; owing to the fact that
explanation: ことから presents a fact as the grounds you reason from — 'from the fact that A, we can tell / it came about that B.' It often explains how a conclusion is reached, or how a name or reputation arose. The B clause is a judgment, result, or naming that follows from A.

related.note: から states a straightforward reason; ことから presents a fact as evidence you draw a conclusion from.
ので gives an objective cause for a result; ことから emphasizes reasoning outward from a known fact.
ことだから reasons from someone's known character; ことから reasons from an observed fact or circumstance.

meanings: entirely; every last one; without exception
explanation: ことごとく is a formal adverb meaning that something applies to every single item with no exceptions: 提案がことごとく否決された = every last proposal was voted down. It typically sweeps over a set of things (plans, predictions, buildings) and very often the outcome is unwelcome — everything failed, everything was destroyed. In kanji it is 悉く, but it is normally written in kana. It belongs to written and news-report style; casual speech prefers 全部 or すべて.

related.note: 〜ごとく means 'like, as if' and is a different word entirely — don't let the shared kana mislead you.
まるっきり means 'utterly, completely' about degree; ことごとく counts through every member of a set.

meanings: cannot do ~ even though one wants to; be stuck unable to ~
explanation: This pattern repeats one verb as dictionary form ＋に＋ its potential negative to say the speaker is unable to do it despite wanting to: 言うに言えない = can't bring myself to say it, 引くに引けない = can't back out now. It portrays a bind — the will is there but circumstances block the action. The verbs are limited to ones that form this pair naturally (言う, 引く, 泣く, 帰る, etc.).

synonyms.note: ようにも〜ない builds on the volitional (〜ようにも〜れない); 〜に〜ない uses the dictionary form + に + potential negative for the same 'can't, though I want to'.

meanings: emphasis / informing particle
explanation: よ at the end of a sentence tells the listener something you think they don't already know, or drives your point home — like adding "you know" or "I'm telling you". It presents new information or reassurance from the speaker to the listener.

related.note: ね seeks the listener's agreement; よ informs them of something new.

meanings: once (one does); for the moment; temporarily
explanation: 一旦 has two related uses. First, 'once ~ (has happened), then ...', setting up a condition after which a state holds — 一旦決めたら = once you've decided (it's hard to reverse). Second, 'for the moment / temporarily', marking a provisional pause — 一旦中止する = suspend for now. It is fairly formal and common in writing and announcements.

related.note: 一応 means 'tentatively / just in case'; 一旦 means 'once (one does)' or 'temporarily'.

surface: かとおもったら・かとおもうと
reading: かとおもったら・かとおもうと
meanings: just when; no sooner had ~ than; and then, unexpectedly
structure: Verb［plain form］＋ かと思ったら／かと思うと
Sentence ＋ かと思ったら／かと思うと
explanation: [plain form] + かと思ったら / かと思うと links two events in quick succession, where the second is often surprising or the opposite of what the first would lead you to expect: 'just when I thought X, (to my surprise) Y'. The speaker is describing something observed, not planning it.

synonyms.note: か〜ないかのうちに also marks 'barely had X happened when Y', but focuses purely on the near-simultaneous timing without the note of surprise.
た途端 means 'the moment after', usually a sudden event; かと思ったら adds that the second thing runs counter to expectation.

related.note: かと思いきや is a more literary cousin stressing that reality contradicted a mistaken assumption; かと思ったら is the everyday form.

meanings: should ~; it'd be good if ~; you can just ~
explanation: 〜ばいい suggests that doing something is a good idea or the way to solve a problem — 分からなければ、先生に聞けばいい = if you don't understand, you can just ask the teacher. It can give advice ('you should just…'), state a solution, or express a wish (雨が止めばいい = I hope the rain stops). The ば-form carries the 'if you do it' sense and いい adds 'that would be good'.

related.note: 〜方がいい compares and recommends one option; 〜ばいい points to doing something as the good move or solution.
the 〜たら conditional can replace ば here (聞いたらいい); both give advice about what to do.
〜ばよかった regrets what you should have done; 〜ばいい advises what is good to do now.

meanings: if you do that; if that's done; in that case
explanation: そうすると takes the previous action or statement as a condition and gives what follows from it — "if you do that, then…" or "in that case." 右に曲がってください。そうすると、駅が見えます = Turn right; if you do that, you'll see the station. It's more explicit than plain すると about supposing "that (action/situation)."

related.note: すると narrates what actually happened next; そうすると sets up "do that → this results."
そこで leads to the speaker's next chosen action; そうすると gives the result of supposing "that."

meanings: it seems that ~ (deduction from evidence)
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ とみえて ＋ Sentence
explanation: 〜とみえる draws a conclusion from what you can observe: 'it seems that ~, judging by the evidence'. 〜とみえて connects that inference to a following clause that shows the evidence or result.

synonyms.note: 〜らしい also infers from evidence but is more colloquial; 〜とみえる is more deductive and literary.

related.note: 〜そうだ reads an appearance directly; 〜とみえる reasons back to a cause.
〜ようだ is a broad 'it seems'; 〜とみえる specifically infers from observed evidence.

surface: なんという・なんと・なんて
reading: なんという・なんと・なんて
meanings: how ~!; what a ~! (exclamation of strong feeling)
structure: なんという／なんと／なんて＋Noun
なんと／なんて＋Adjective＋（だろう／でしょう）
explanation: As exclamations, なんという／なんと／なんて express strong emotion — admiration, astonishment, or dismay — before a noun or adjective: なんて美しい景色だろう = what a beautiful view!, なんという偶然 = what a coincidence. They often round off with だろう／でしょう. なんて is the most colloquial of the three; なんと and なんという feel a little more emphatic or written.

synonyms.note: といったらない conveys an extreme, indescribable degree of feeling; なんという／なんて is a more direct exclamatory 'what a ~!'.

related.note: など (and its colloquial なんて) can dismiss or belittle ('~ and the like / such a thing as'); the exclamatory なんて here voices strong emotion instead.

meanings: to have a ~ experience; to feel ~ (an emotion) keenly
explanation: 〜思いをする describes undergoing an experience colored by a particular feeling, with the feeling word placed before 思い. 悔しい思いをする = go through something galling; つらい思いをする = have a painful experience; 恥ずかしい思いをする = suffer embarrassment. It takes an い-adjective, or a な-adjective + な, before 思い and focuses on how an experience felt to the person.

meanings: to ~ into (inward); to ~ deeply / thoroughly
explanation: 込む attaches to a verb stem in two related senses: moving something inward (飛び込む jump in, 押し込む shove in) and doing an action deeply, hard, or over a long stretch (考え込む sink into thought, 使い込む use extensively). Context makes clear which sense is meant. The compound conjugates as an ordinary う-verb.

antonyms.note: 〜出す points an action outward or marks a sudden start; 込む (in the inward sense) moves things in.

related.note: 〜切る stresses completing an action fully to the end; 込む (thorough sense) stresses doing it deeply or at length.
〜抜く means pushing an action through to the very end despite difficulty; 込む (thorough sense) is doing it intensively or repeatedly.

meanings: even just ~; at least ~
structure: Noun［often a small quantity］＋なりとも
何／誰＋なりと ［fixed: 'anything / anyone at all'］
explanation: 〜なりとも attaches to a (usually small) amount or noun to mean 'even if only ~, at least ~': 多少なりとも = even a little, 少しなりとも = even slightly. It concedes that the amount is minimal while stressing that even that much matters. It is formal or literary, and appears in fixed forms such as 多少なりとも and 何なりと ('anything at all').

related.note: Same syllables なり, different pattern: なり〜なり offers a choice of examples, while 〜なりとも means 'even just ~, at least'.

surface: てばかりはいられない
reading: てばかりはいられない
meanings: can't just keep ~ing (something else needs doing)
structure: Verb［て form］＋ばかりはいられない
explanation: てばかりはいられない combines て + ばかり ('only') + はいられない to say one cannot go on doing just this one thing — 落ち込んでばかりはいられない = 'I can't just keep moping'. It acknowledges the action but insists it can't continue as the only thing, because other responsibilities call. The tone is one of pulling oneself together to move on.

synonyms.note: てはいられない simply says you can't stay as you are; てばかりはいられない stresses you can't do only that one thing.

meanings: about the only ~ is; roughly the extent of it is ~
structure: Topic ＋ は ＋ … ＋ くらいです
explanation: は〜くらいです presents something as the modest limit of what applies — the most you can say, or the only real example. 運動と言えば、犬の散歩くらいです = as for exercise, dog-walking is about the only one. くらい here downplays the amount or degree, framing it as small or the sole case.

related.note: くらい・ぐらい broadly marks approximate amount or degree; は〜くらいです uses it to frame something as the modest limit.
〜しかない flatly limits things to 'nothing but'; は〜くらいです softly presents the modest extent instead.
ほど also scales degree; くらい in this pattern downplays it to 'about the only / that little'.

meanings: sorry for ~ing
structure: Verb［て form］＋ すみません／すみませんでした
explanation: Apologizes for an action you did or are doing: 〜てすみません = 'sorry for ~ing'. For a finished action, use the past 〜てすみませんでした. More casual is 〜てごめん(なさい). It mirrors てくれてありがとう, but as an apology rather than thanks.

meanings: there's a limit to; ~ goes too far
structure: Verb［plain form］／い-adjective／な-adjective＋にもほどがある
explanation: 〜にもほどがある is a sharp criticism that some behavior has crossed the bounds of what's acceptable — 冗談にもほどがある = there's a limit to joking, 失礼にもほどがある = that's rude beyond all limits. meanings: all the more because; being the case, naturally
structure: Noun／Verb・い-adjective・な-adjective［plain form］ ＋ だけに ［な-adjective takes な］
explanation: だけに says that because a condition holds strongly, the result is all the greater or all the more understandable — 'being ~, all the more so'. Unlike だけあって, the outcome can be positive or negative, including heightened disappointment.

meanings: with ~ close ahead; on the eve of
explanation: 〜を控えて describes a situation in which an important event is imminent, and the main clause tells what is happening in the run-up: 試験を控えて猛勉強する = cram with exams looming; 出発を明日に控えて = with departure the next day. Here 控える means 'have (something) close ahead', temporally (or sometimes spatially). The impending event is usually significant, which colors the preparation or mood.

related.note: に先立ち = doing something in advance of an event; を控えて = being in the run-up with the event looming ahead.
にあたって marks the occasion of doing something; を控えて sets the scene of an imminent event and what happens before it.

meanings: as if to say ~; with a manner that all but says ~
explanation: 〜とばかりに attaches a quoted thought to someone's behavior: they don't actually speak the words, but their manner or action conveys them — 'as if to say ~'. 帰れとばかりに、彼はドアを指さした = he pointed at the door as if to say 'get out'. It often accompanies a vivid gesture or a decisive move, and captures the attitude the person is broadcasting without words.

meanings: it is said that ~
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ と言われている
explanation: 〜と言われている reports what people in general say or believe, with no named source: 'it is said that ~'. The passive 言われる ('is said') plus ている presents the statement as widely held.

synonyms.note: 〜とされている is more official-sounding; 〜と言われている is everyday hearsay.

related.note: 〜と考えられている implies a reasoned conclusion; 〜と言われている is just what people say.
〜そうだ also reports hearsay but usually from a specific recent source.

meanings: due to; per; each
explanation: につき has two main uses. As 'due to', it gives a reason in formal notices — 本日は定休日につき休業します ('as today is a regular holiday, we are closed'). As 'per', it states a rate — 一つにつき百円 ('100 yen each'). Both are set, somewhat formal uses of the same につき.

synonyms.note: 当たり covers the 'per unit' rate sense; につき shares that sense but also means 'due to', which 当たり never does.

related.note: ために gives a reason in ordinary registers; につき in its 'due to' sense is the stiffer, notice-style equivalent.

meanings: good at doing ~
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋ のが ＋ 上手（です）
explanation: To say someone is skilled at an activity, nominalize the verb with の, mark it with が, and finish with 上手. It describes a learned ability, so it fits things like cooking, singing, or a language.

antonyms.note: のが下手 says someone is bad at an activity; のが上手 says they are good at it.

related.note: Same のが frame, but 好き is about liking the activity rather than being skilled.
ことができる states plain ability (can do); のが上手 rates the quality of that skill.

meanings: in short; to sum up; essentially
explanation: 要するに is an adverbial phrase that introduces a concise restatement of what was just said — 'in short, essentially, to put it briefly'. The speaker boils a longer account down to its core point, often cutting through detail to the conclusion that really matters.

synonyms.note: つまり restates 'in other words'; 要するに specifically frames the restatement as a boiled-down summary of the essentials.
ということだ concludes 'it amounts to ~'; 要するに opens the sentence to signal a summary is coming.

meanings: only; just; a mere
explanation: たった emphasizes that a quantity is surprisingly small — 'only this much, a mere ~'. The optional の comes before the number (たったの千円). It stresses that the amount falls short of expectation, often with disappointment or to underline how little there is.

synonyms.note: だけ is a neutral 'only'; たった adds emphatic surprise at how small the amount is.
のみ is a formal 'only' without the emotional stress; たった dramatizes the smallness.

related.note: ばかり with a number gives an approximate amount ('about'); たった pins down an exact, strikingly small figure.

meanings: on the assumption that; treating (something) as being the case
structure: Verb［た form］／Verb［ない form］＋ものとして
explanation: 〜ものとして means 'treating ~ as (settled/true)', proceeding on a stated premise even if it is not literally confirmed. 合意したものとして進める = proceed as though agreement has been reached; なかったものとして扱う = treat it as if it never happened. It attaches to a plain-form clause and works adverbially to set the assumption on which the following action is based.

synonyms.note: ものとする is a declaration ('shall be / is deemed'); ものとして adverbially sets the premise for a following action.

related.note: ものと思う states what the speaker assumes to be true; ものとして proceeds as if it is true, whether or not it actually is.

meanings: only; just; (after た-form) ~ and nothing since
explanation: きり has two senses: after a noun it means 'only, just' (二人きり = just the two of us), and after a た-form verb it means 'since ~, and nothing has changed since' (出かけたきり = went out and hasn't come back). Both narrow things down to a single case.

synonyms.note: だけ 'only' is the neutral limiter; きり is more exclusive/colloquial and also has the た-form 'since' use.

related.note: ばかり 'nothing but / just' overlaps in the 'only' sense; きり adds the 'and nothing since' meaning.

meanings: na-adjective modifying a noun (~な＋noun)
explanation: Puts a な-adjective in front of a noun to describe it: insert な between the adjective and the noun. This な is exactly what gives these adjectives their name, and it appears only in this attributive position.

related.note: Uses だ／です instead of な when the adjective ends the sentence.
い-adjectives attach straight to the noun with no extra な.
A noun needs の to modify another noun, where a な-adjective uses な.

meanings: rather than ~; more like B than A
explanation: 〜というより refines how you describe one thing, saying B is a more accurate label than A — 優しいというより気が弱い = not so much kind as timid. It compares two descriptions of the same thing and is often followed by むしろ ('rather').

synonyms.note: ではなくて flatly rejects A for B; というより softens it to 'B is the more fitting way to put it'.

related.note: より alone compares two separate things; というより compares two labels for the same thing.

that's why; so that means; it follows that
explanation: 〜というわけだ presents the current statement as the natural conclusion or restatement that follows from what was just said — 'so that means ~, that's how it is'. It either draws a logical upshot (終電を逃した、というわけだ = so that's why...) or rephrases a situation more plainly, and the listener is expected to see it as the sensible conclusion of the preceding context.

synonyms.note: わけだ draws the conclusion directly; というわけだ frames the whole preceding statement as the thing that leads to it, often when restating.
ということだ can report hearsay or sum up a meaning; というわけだ specifically presents a reasoned upshot of the context.

related.note: つまり cues a restatement or summary; というわけだ closes the sentence by presenting it as the logical conclusion.

meanings: you could say ~; one might say ~
structure: Sentence／Noun［plain form］＋ と言ってもいい
explanation: 〜と言ってもいい means 'you could say that ~' or 'it's fair to say ~'. It lets you put forward a strong or bold characterization while framing it as one acceptable way to describe something, softening the claim.

related.note: 〜と言っても alone is concessive ('even though you say'); adding いい makes it 'you may say'.
Both use 言う; と言ってもいい offers a description as acceptable, という attaches a name.

meanings: and yet; even so; despite that
explanation: それなのに opens a sentence to say the result clashes with what the previous statement would lead you to expect — 'and yet, in spite of that'. It carries surprise, dissatisfaction, or complaint about the contradictory outcome.

synonyms.note: それでも concedes the previous point and pushes on; それなのに reacts with surprise or complaint at the contradiction.

related.note: のに joins the contrast within one sentence; それなのに links two sentences.
にもかかわらず is a formal 'despite'; それなのに is conversational and more emotional.
くせに contrasts with reproach and only about a person; それなのに applies to any situation.

meanings: surely ~ (and yet); would ~ if only (regret, sympathy, or reproach)
explanation: だろうに follows a plain-form clause to state what would surely be true under some — usually counterfactual — condition, while the actual situation falls short, leaving a feeling of pity, regret, or mild reproach. 早く言ってくれれば助けられただろうに = if you had told me sooner I could have helped you (but you didn't). The に carries the unspoken 'and yet…'. It often follows a conditional, and the disappointing reality is frequently left implied.

synonyms.note: ものを also voices regret that reality went against a preferable hypothetical, but is more literary and reproachful; だろうに centers on the speaker's 'surely it would have…' inference.

related.note: plain だろう is a conjecture ('probably'); adding に turns it into wistful regret or reproach about how things could have been.
のに contrasts an actual result with expectation; だろうに contrasts a desirable hypothetical with a disappointing, often counterfactual, reality.

meanings: not until you first do; can't unless you do first
structure: Verb［て form］＋ からでないと／からでなければ ＋ （negative）
explanation: 〜てからでないと sets a required first step — nothing further can happen until it's done. It's usually followed by a negative outcome: 予約してからでないと入れない = you can't get in unless you book first. Literally 'if it isn't after doing ~.'

related.note: てから simply means 'after doing'; てからでないと adds that nothing else is possible until then.
なければならない states that an action is necessary; てからでないと makes that action a prerequisite for something else.

meanings: long ago; already (a long time back)
explanation: とっくに is a casual adverb meaning something happened well before now — 'long ago / already (ages ago)'. とっくに終わったよ = 'it finished ages ago'. It stresses that the event lies far in the past relative to the moment being discussed, often with mild surprise the listener didn't already know.

synonyms.note: すでに is the neutral, more formal 'already'; とっくに is casual and stresses that it was a long time ago.

related.note: もう marks 'already' at or by now; とっくに pushes the timing well back into the past.

surface: ものとおもわれる・ものとみられる
reading: ものとおもわれる・ものとみられる
meanings: it is thought that; it is expected/estimated that
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ものと思われる／ものと見られる
explanation: 〜ものと思われる and 〜ものと見られる give a detached, objective judgment — 'it is thought / it is believed that ~'. The passive removes any single speaker, so these are staples of news reports, official statements, and academic writing: 原因は漏電によるものと見られる = the cause is believed to be an electrical short. They attach to a plain-form clause and present a cautious, evidence-based inference rather than a personal opinion.

synonyms.note: ものと思う states the speaker's own assumption; ものと思われる is the impersonal passive 'it is thought that'.
に違いない is a confident 'must be'; ものと思われる is a cautious, hedged inference typical of reporting.

meanings: as soon as; the moment (one does) ~

explanation: Verb［dictionary form］＋なり means the second action follows the very instant the first is done: 家に帰るなり寝てしまった = the moment he got home, he fell asleep. related.note: か〜ないかのうちに says the second event began before the first fully finished; なり has the first clearly complete, then the reaction right after.

meanings: roughly; approximately; generally; (with a negative) utterly
explanation: およそ has a few uses. Before a number it means 'roughly, about': およそ千人 = about a thousand people. As a sentence adverb it means 'generally speaking, in broad terms': およそ物事には順序がある = in general, things have an order. Reinforcing a negative, it means 'utterly, not in the least': およそ現実的でない = utterly unrealistic. Context and what follows tell the senses apart.

synonyms.note: おおよそ is essentially the same word in the 'roughly / approximately' sense; およそ additionally carries the emphatic 'utterly (not)' use.

meanings: therefore; hence; because of; for the reason that (formal)
explanation: ゆえに expresses cause and consequence in formal, literary, or logical language. As a conjunction at the head of a sentence it means 'therefore, hence'. Attached to a noun (＋ゆえ／のゆえに) or a plain clause (＋がゆえに) it means 'owing to ~, because of ~': 経験の浅さゆえに = owing to inexperience. It is the register of reasoned argument and classical style, far more formal than から or ので.

synonyms.note: から is the everyday 'because'; ゆえに expresses the same causal link in formal, literary, or logical writing.
ため(に) gives a neutral cause or purpose; ゆえに is more formal and belongs to reasoned or classical style.

related.note: ので softens a reason as objective and polite; ゆえに is markedly formal and literary.

meanings: like ~; similar to ~ (resemblance/example)
structure: Noun ＋ みたいに ＋ Verb ／ Adjective
explanation: みたいな and みたいに express resemblance — 'like / similar to' a given example. みたいな modifies a noun (夢みたいな話, a dream-like story), while みたいに modifies a verb or adjective (子どもみたいに笑う, laugh like a child). It's the casual counterpart of ような・ように.

synonyms.note: ような・ように is the formal equivalent; みたいな・みたいに is the casual, conversational form.

related.note: みたいだ ends a sentence as a guess ('seems like'); みたいな・みたいに says 'like/similar to'.

meanings: in accordance with; in line with (facts, reality, rules)
explanation: 〜に即して means acting in keeping with a concrete standard such as the facts, reality, law, or one's experience — 'in line with ~, grounded in ~'. 現実に即した対策 = measures grounded in reality, 規則に即して判断する = judge in accordance with the rules. It stresses fitting one's response to how things actually are, not to abstract ideals. The adnominal form is に即した, and the register is formal.

synonyms.note: に照らして checks something against a standard or precedent to judge it; に即して means shaping one's response to fit the actual facts.

related.note: に基づいて uses something as a foundation or grounds to build on; に即して means staying faithful to the concrete facts or rules.
に沿って means following along a line, plan, or wish; に即して means conforming to how things actually are.

meanings: after doing ~ and then; upon ~; in the course of ~
explanation: With the past form or a noun + の, 〜上で means 'after deliberately doing X, then do Y' — 相談した上で = after discussing it, then… . With the dictionary form it means 'in the course of / for the purpose of' (生きる上で = in living / in life). The 'after' use marks a considered step taken before the next action.

related.note: 〜てから is the everyday 'after doing'; 〜た上で is more formal and stresses X as a deliberate step taken before Y.
〜後で just orders two events in time; 〜た上で implies you do X on purpose as a basis for doing Y.

meanings: (I heard) something like ~; and reportedly because ~
explanation: とか, and especially とかで, reports something heard in a vague, non-committal way — '(I heard) something like ~'. とかで adds a reported reason: 熱があるとかで休んだ = 'he was off, apparently because he had a fever or something'. The speaker signals the information is secondhand and imprecise.

synonyms.note: そうだ reports hearsay as heard; とかで is vaguer ('something like') and adds a reported reason with で.

related.note: ということだ reports information as a clear conclusion or definition; とかで keeps it deliberately vague and secondhand.
らしい draws a conjecture from what one has heard; とかで simply relays the vague report as a reason.

meanings: at least ~ is better; it could have been worse
structure: Verb・い-adjective［plain form］ ＋ だけましだ
Noun ＋ な ＋ だけましだ
explanation: だけましだ says that although the situation is bad, it could have been worse, so one saving grace makes it 'at least better than nothing'. まし means 'the lesser evil', so the tone is resigned relief rather than genuine satisfaction.

synonyms.note: ほうがましだ compares two bad options and picks the less bad; だけましだ finds a redeeming point within one situation.

related.note: せめて wishes for a bare minimum; だけましだ accepts a small consolation already gained.

meanings: what with ~ and ~ (listing burdens or complaints)
explanation: やれ〜やれ〜 lists one troublesome thing after another, usually with a tone of exasperation at how much is piling up: やれ会議だやれ報告書だ = what with meetings and reports and everything. Each item is often a noun + だ, and the string is frequently rounded off with と before a verb like 忙しい. It conveys the speaker's weariness at a barrage of demands, and is colloquial.

related.note: なり〜なり lists alternatives to choose from ('either A or B'); やれ〜やれ lists grievances piling up, with a weary tone.

meanings: compared to; in comparison with ~
explanation: に比べて sets a baseline you measure something against — 'compared to ~'. 去年に比べて雨が多い ('there's more rain compared to last year'), 都会に比べて田舎は安い ('the countryside is cheaper compared to the city'). The noun before に比べて is the reference point; the new information comes in the main clause. に比べ is the same, a touch more formal.

synonyms.note: より marks the standard in a plain comparison ('than'); に比べて frames a broader 'compared with'.

related.note: に対して sets two things in direct contrast; に比べて weighs one against a baseline.
わりに means 'considering / for (what you'd expect)'; に比べて is a straight comparison.

meanings: looking like; smacking of (something undesirable)
explanation: 〜じみた, from the verb 染みる ('to soak into'), says something has taken on the unwelcome look or air of a noun: 子供じみた態度 = a childish attitude, 芝居じみた言い訳 = a theatrical excuse. The judgment is always negative — the thing resembles something it shouldn't. It attaches to a limited set of nouns (子供, 芝居, 狂気, 説教, 年寄り...), modifies nouns as じみた, and predicates as じみている.

synonyms.note: っぽい is colloquial, freely productive, and can be neutral; じみた is critical and limited to set nouns.
めく says something 'has an air of' fairly neutrally (春めく); じみた always disapproves of the resemblance.

related.note: らしい affirms something shows its proper, expected character; じみた accuses it of an improper resemblance.

meanings: from the standpoint of ~; in terms of ~; for ~ reasons
explanation: Noun＋上 (じょう) means 'from the standpoint of ~ / in terms of ~' — 法律上 = legally, 健康上 = for health reasons, 立場上 = given one's position. It frames the following statement within that particular domain or consideration. It attaches to a limited set of abstract nouns.

synonyms.note: 的 turns a noun into '~-wise / in terms of ~' broadly; 〜上 is limited to fixed nouns and often means 'from the standpoint of'.

related.note: 上で reads うえで and means 'upon doing / in the course of'; the same kanji, but a different reading and meaning.

meanings: X is famous for ~
structure: Noun ＋ は ＋ Noun ＋ で有名（だ）
Verb［plain form］＋ ことで有名（だ）
explanation: 〜は〜で有名です says what something is well known for — その町はお茶で有名です = that town is famous for its tea. The で marks the reason or feature it is famous for. To say 'famous for doing something', nominalize the verb with こと first: 早く走ることで有名だ.

related.note: 〜として marks the role or capacity something is known in; 〜で有名 marks the feature it is famous for.

meanings: I wonder ~ (feminine)
explanation: かしら is a sentence-ending particle for musing to yourself — 'I wonder ~'. 来るかしら = I wonder if they'll come. It attaches to the plain form and carries a soft, feminine tone in modern speech.

synonyms.note: かな is the same 'I wonder', but neutral/masculine where かしら is feminine.

related.note: かい asks the listener a casual yes/no question; かしら wonders to oneself.
でしょう guesses with some confidence; かしら voices genuine, softer uncertainty.

meanings: no matter what/who/how ~; whatever ~ may be
structure: Question word＋であれ／であろうと
explanation: After a question word (or a noun paired with one), であれ and であろうと concede that the outcome holds regardless — どんな事情であれ = whatever the circumstances, 誰であろうと = no matter who it is. であろうと adds a slightly stronger 'even supposing' nuance. Both are the concessive of である and belong to formal or written Japanese; the main clause states what applies in every case.

synonyms.note: であれ〜であれ lists two named alternatives; single であれ pairs with a question word for 'no matter what'.
ようが／ようと concedes over verbs and adjectives ('no matter how one does'); であれ concedes over a noun or question word.
いかなる〜であれ／であろうと is a set formal pairing; であれ supplies the concession that いかなる ('any whatsoever') modifies.

related.note: 〜ても is the basic 'even if'; であれ／であろうと is its formal noun-based counterpart for 'whatever it may be'.

meanings: so as never to; to make sure ~ never happens
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋ことのないように
explanation: 〜ことのないように wraps a feared event in ことのない ('such that it never happens') and aims an action at preventing it: 二度と起こることのないように対策する = take measures so it never happens again. It is the formal, emphatic version of plain ないように, common in official apologies, announcements, and warnings, and frequently reinforced with 二度と ('never again'). The main clause states the precaution or request.

synonyms.note: Plain ように expresses the same purpose neutrally; ことのないように adds formal weight and the sense of 'never'.

related.note: べからず bluntly prohibits on signs; ことのないように politely urges prevention.

surface: きわまる・きわまりない
reading: きわまる・きわまりない
meanings: extremely; utterly; in the highest degree
explanation: 〜極まる and 〜極まりない both attach to a な-adjective stem and mean 'extremely, utterly ~', describing a quality pushed to its limit: 失礼極まりない (extremely rude), 危険極まる (utterly dangerous). Curiously, despite the ない, 極まりない means the same as 極まる — both are affirmative in force. The pattern is formal, emphatic, and often voices strong disapproval or strong feeling in written style.

synonyms.note: の極み attaches to a noun and names 'the very height of ~'; 極まる／極まりない attach to a な-adjective quality.
限りだ conveys the speaker's own feeling at its utmost (嬉しい限りだ); 極まりない more often condemns an external quality.

related.note: の至り expresses an emotion or state reaching its extreme, often in set humble phrases; 極まる rates a described quality as extreme.

meanings: gradually; by degrees; steadily
explanation: 次第に is an adverb meaning 'gradually, little by little'. It describes a change that unfolds step by step — 空が次第に暗くなった = the sky gradually darkened. It is a somewhat formal, written-flavored synonym of だんだん.

synonyms.note: だんだん is the everyday 'gradually'; 次第に is more formal and written.
つつある is 'in the process of ~ing', framing an ongoing change; 次第に is an adverb describing how the change proceeds.

related.note: 次第で shares the kanji but means 'depending on', attaching to a noun; 次第に is 'gradually'.

surface: だれか・どこか・だれも・どこも
reading: だれか・どこか・だれも・どこも
meanings: someone/somewhere; no one/nowhere
structure: 誰／どこ／何 ＋ も ＋ Verb［ない form］
explanation: Builds indefinite words from question words: 誰/どこ/何 plus か gives "someone / somewhere / something", while the same words plus も with a negative verb give "no one / nowhere / nothing". Learners use these to speak vaguely when they don't know or don't need to specify who or where.

related.note: 何か・何も (something / nothing) is the same family built on 何 for things rather than people or places.

meanings: that said; even so; nonetheless
explanation: 〜とはいえ concedes a point and then states something that runs contrary to what that point would lead you to expect — 'even though ~, still ...'. It is more formal and written than とはいうものの, and can either join clauses or open a sentence as 'Nonetheless, ...'. 便利とはいえ、頼りすぎは良くない = convenient though it is, relying on it too much is bad. The main clause qualifies or resists the conceded premise.

synonyms.note: とはいうものの is nearly identical in meaning, slightly softer and more conversational.

related.note: ものの concedes within a single sentence ('although'); とはいえ can stand alone as a sentence-opening 'nonetheless'.
ながらも concedes about one subject's own action or state ('even while ~ing'); とはいえ concedes a whole statement.

surface: にいたる・にいたって・にいたり
reading: にいたる・にいたって・にいたり
meanings: to reach (an extreme point or final state); only when it came to ~
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋に至る／に至って／に至り
Noun＋に至る／に至って／に至り
explanation: 〜に至る describes finally arriving at an extreme, serious, or final stage after a long process — much weightier than plain なる. 合併するに至る = to reach the point of merging, ここに至る = to come to this pass. The connective 至って marks 'upon finally reaching ~', and 至り appears in formal writing. It stresses that things went all the way to a decisive end. The register is formal and literary.

related.note: に至るまで stresses a range extending even to an extreme endpoint; に至る marks arriving at a final stage after a process.
に至っては singles out one extreme case for comment; に至る simply states reaching an extreme point.
に至っても concedes 'even having reached (that point), still ~'; に至る just marks the reaching itself.

meanings: which means; that is to say; so that means
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ ということは
explanation: ということは takes a known fact or statement and draws the logical conclusion that follows from it — 'which means / so that means'. 電気がついているということは = 'the lights are on, which means...'. It often stands at the head of a sentence as a connector (ということは、〜) to walk the listener through an inference.

synonyms.note: つまり restates the same content more simply ('in other words'); ということは derives a fresh consequence from it.

related.note: ということだ reports what was heard or defines a term; ということは reasons out what a fact implies.
というわけだ presents the resulting explanation ('that's why'); ということは explicitly walks through the inference to reach it.

meanings: no one/nothing but; none other than
explanation: 〜をおいて〜ない singles out X as the one and only option, ending in a negative: 彼をおいて適任者はいない = there is no one suited but him. The をおいて here means 'setting aside / other than', and ほかに is often inserted (をおいてほかにない). It carries strong positive evaluation, presenting X as uniquely qualified with no real alternative.

synonyms.note: を除いて simply excludes X from a set; をおいて〜ない goes further, saying X is the sole option and nothing else qualifies.

related.note: ならでは also stresses uniqueness ('only X can'), but as a positive attribute of X; をおいて〜ない frames it through a negation of all alternatives.

related.note: Sounds close but ついに means 'finally, at last'; つい means 'without meaning to.'

meanings: or; or else (offering a choice in a question)
structure: Noun ＋ それとも ＋ Noun（within a question）
explanation: それとも sits between two questions or options and asks the listener to choose — "or (is it) ...?" It belongs in questions where you lay out alternatives, not in plain statements.

meanings: but; because (excuse); also 'even; too'

meanings: unbearably ~; can't stand how ~; dying to ~
explanation: てたまらない expresses a feeling or desire so strong the speaker can hardly bear it — 暑くてたまらない = 'unbearably hot', 会いたくてたまらない = 'dying to see someone'. It attaches to the て-form of adjectives and verbs of emotion or sensation. たまらない literally means 'cannot be endured', so the whole phrase conveys an overwhelming, uncontrollable state.

synonyms.note: てならない conveys the same overwhelming feeling but leans formal and favors spontaneous thoughts (思えてならない).
てしょうがない・てしかたがない is the more casual 'can't help feeling'; てたまらない stresses that the feeling is barely bearable.

meanings: disregarding; ignoring; without regard to
explanation: 〜をよそに attaches to a noun — usually someone's worry, opposition, or concern — and says the subject went ahead as if it were none of their business. 親の心配をよそに (heedless of his parents' worry), 周囲の反対をよそに (ignoring everyone's objections). The nuance is often critical: the subject coolly brushes aside something they really ought to have taken into account. It is written and formal in flavor.

related.note: をものともせず admiringly overcomes a hardship; をよそに coolly, often selfishly, disregards concern one ought to weigh.
にもかかわらず neutrally says 'despite the fact that'; をよそに specifically shrugs off others' feelings or objections.

meanings: as ~ as possible; if possible
explanation: なるべく is an adverb meaning 'as much as possible' or 'if you can'. Place it before a verb, adjective, or whole clause to say you want that done to the greatest extent circumstances allow: なるべく早く = as early as possible. It softens a wish or instruction into 'do your best to ~' rather than a hard demand.

structure: Verb［ない form, drop ない］＋ ざる

explanation: 〜ざる is a classical negative ending equal to 〜ない before a noun. It survives in modern written and set expressions — 絶えざる努力 = ceaseless effort, 予期せざる事態 = an unforeseen situation. It attaches to the ない-form base (the あ-stem) of a verb, with する → せざる and くる → こざる. Mostly literary or fixed-phrase, not everyday speech.

synonyms.note: 〜ぬ is the classical negative that ends a clause or precedes a noun; 〜ざる is a parallel attributive form.

related.note: ざるを得ない ('have no choice but') is built on this same ざる base, fixed with を得ない.

meanings: why; how come
structure: どうして ＋ Sentence ＋ か／の？
explanation: Asks for a reason: put どうして at the start of a question to ask why something is the case. It is neutral and very common in everyday conversation, and the answer is usually given with から or ので.

synonyms.note: なぜ asks 'why' in a more formal or written tone; どうして is everyday and conversational.
なんで is the casual, spoken 'why'; どうして is neutral and slightly more polite.

related.note: どうやって asks 'by what method'; どうして asks 'for what reason'.

meanings: still; even now; to this day
explanation: 未だに stresses that a state has persisted unchanged right up to the present, usually with a note of surprise or dissatisfaction that it has not changed — 未だに返事がない = still no reply even now. It carries the nuance that the situation really ought to have changed by this point. It is stronger and more formal than a plain まだ, and often appears with a negative or 〜ている.

meanings: via; through; after (a process or interval)
explanation: 〜を経て marks passing through a stage, place, or span of time on the way to a result: 長い交渉を経て合意に達した = reached agreement after long negotiations; パリを経てロンドンへ = via Paris to London. 経て is the て-form of 経る 'to pass through'. It is formal and written, emphasizing the intervening process that led to the final state.

synonyms.note: を通じて = by means of, or throughout a span; を経て = after passing through a stage on the way to a result.

related.note: た末に stresses a final outcome after much effort/trouble; を経て neutrally marks the process or stages passed through.

meanings: ~ and ~ (linking adjectives and nouns)
explanation: Links two descriptions in one sentence, meaning "and". Change an い-adjective's ending to くて, and put で after a noun or な-adjective, to connect it smoothly to the next part. It lets you stack qualities without starting a new sentence.

related.note: そして joins two whole sentences; くて・で links descriptions inside a single sentence.
Same い-adjective conjugation family — くない is the negative, くて the connective form.

meanings: without caring about ~; heedless of ~; paying no mind to ~
structure: Sentence ＋ の ＋ もかまわず
explanation: 〜もかまわず (も構わず) means acting without concern for something that would normally give one pause — 人目もかまわず ('heedless of others' eyes'). The doer goes ahead despite X, ignoring what X would ordinarily demand.

related.note: にもかかわらず means 'despite (a fact)'; もかまわず stresses that the doer pays X no mind.
を問わず means 'regardless of which/any'; もかまわず means acting without heeding one specific concern.

meanings: have no choice but to; no option besides
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋ よりほかない／よりほかはない
explanation: 〜よりほかない (also よりほかはない) attaches to a dictionary-form verb to say there is nothing besides doing it — 'no choice but to ~'. It marks the sole remaining option with a tone of resignation, when no better alternative is available.

synonyms.note: よりしかたがない means the same 'no choice but to'; the two are interchangeable in most contexts.
ざるを得ない is a more formal, written way to say one cannot help but do the action.

related.note: 〜しかない likewise limits things to one option; よりほかない adds a resigned, no-alternative nuance.

meanings: I hope that ~; I would appreciate it if ~ (soft, humble wish)
structure: Verb［ば form］＋ と思います
Verb［ば form］＋ （いい）＋ と思います
explanation: A conditional clause ending in ば followed by と思います voices a soft, humble hope — literally 'I think it would be good if…'. The いい ('would be good') after ば is usually left out, so 〜ばと思います on its own reads as a polite 'I hope / I'd be grateful if'. It is common in requests, notices, and speeches.

synonyms.note: ばいい plainly states 'it'd be good if'; 〜ばと思います wraps that in 思う for a humbler, more indirect wish.

related.note: てほしい directly says 'I want you to …'; 〜ばと思います is softer and more deferential.
the と思う here is the ordinary 'I think', which turns a conditional into a modest hope.

meanings: doesn't count as; can hardly be called (a real ~)
explanation: 〜うちに入らない says that something falls short of qualifying as a full or proper example of a category — 'that doesn't count as ~'. この程度の雨なら降ったうちに入らない = a little rain like this hardly counts as rain; 一度会っただけでは知り合いのうちに入らない = meeting once doesn't make you acquaintances. It dismisses the case as too slight to bear that label.

related.note: 〜にすぎない says something is 'no more than ~'; うちに入らない says it doesn't even qualify as ~.

meanings: if one were to (even slightly) do ~, dire consequences would follow
explanation: 〜ようものなら takes a volitional-form verb and warns that if that action were so much as attempted, something serious or disastrous would happen. The consequence is heavy and often exaggerated: 少しでも文句を言おうものなら大変なことになる = if you dared to complain even a little, all hell would break loose. It expresses the speaker's sense that the situation is so touchy that the smallest move triggers an outsized reaction.

synonyms.note: The potential-based ものなら (できるものなら) expresses a wish 'if only one could'; ようものなら uses the volitional to warn of dire results.

meanings: even if; even though
explanation: ても sets up 'even if / even though' — the second clause holds regardless of the first. It attaches to the て form: 食べても, 高くても, 学生でも. It covers both the hypothetical ('even if it rains') and the actual ('even though I studied').

related.note: 〜てもいい grants permission ('may'); ても alone means 'even if'.
でも is the particle 'even'; in the ても pattern, nouns and な-adjectives likewise take でも.

meanings: keeps only getting ~ (a one-way change, usually for the worse)
explanation: A dictionary-form change verb plus ばかりだ says a situation keeps moving in a single direction, with nothing to stop it — 病気は悪くなるばかりだ = the illness just keeps getting worse. It usually carries a negative, worsening tone: things go on changing one way only. The verb is a change verb in dictionary form.

related.note: 〜一方だ also marks a one-way change; 〜ばかりだ adds the sense that nothing stops or improves it.
〜たばかり means 'just did (moments ago)'; 〜ばかりだ with the dictionary form means a situation keeps changing one way.
〜ばかりで lists 'only this, nothing else'; 〜ばかりだ marks a steady one-way change.

meanings: transitive and intransitive verb pairs
explanation: Japanese has many verb pairs: a 他動詞 (transitive), where someone acts on a thing marked with を, and a matching 自動詞 (intransitive), where the thing changes by itself and is marked with が. 開ける/開く, 閉める/閉まる, and 消す/消える are classic pairs you learn together.

related.note: 〜てある pairs with a transitive verb to show a state someone set up on purpose.
〜ている with an intransitive verb shows the state that resulted.
The passive also drops the doer, but reshapes を→が differently from an intransitive pair.

meanings: to look ~; to appear ~ (judging from how it looks)
structure: Verb／い-adjective［plain form］＋ ように見える
な-adjective ＋ な／Noun ＋ の ＋ ように見える
explanation: 〜ように見える says something looks or appears a certain way to the observer, based on its visible appearance — 本物のように見える = looks like the real thing. The judgment comes from what you can actually see.

related.note: ようだ is a broad 'it seems' from any evidence; ように見える specifically means 'looks like' by sight.
みたいだ is the casual 'seems'; ように見える is more clearly tied to visible appearance.
ような気がする is a felt impression; ように見える is what your eyes tell you.

meanings: is regarded as; is held to be; is said to be
explanation: 〜とされる presents something as what is generally held, established, or officially regarded to be the case — 'is considered ~, is deemed ~'. 健康に良いとされる = is held to be good for one's health, 最古とされる = regarded as the oldest. The judgment is attributed to society, authorities, or general consensus rather than the speaker's own view. It is common in explanatory, academic, and news writing; とされている stresses the ongoing established state.

synonyms.note: そうだ (hearsay) reports 'I hear that ~' from a specific source; とされる presents an established, widely-held judgment.

related.note: The passive れる/られる underlies とされる; on its own it marks who is affected, while とされる specifically frames a view as generally accepted.

meanings: it is necessary to ~; need to ~
explanation: 必要 means 'necessity', so 〜必要がある states that doing something is necessary — 'there's a need to ~'. A verb in dictionary form plus 必要がある says an action is required; a noun takes が directly (Noun＋が必要). The negative 必要はない means 'there's no need to'.

related.note: なければならない is a firmer 'must'; 必要がある states a plainer factual need.
なくてはいけない stresses an obligation you can't avoid; 必要がある simply notes what's required.
べきだ gives a 'should' based on what's right; 必要がある points to a practical necessity.

surface: にあたって・にあたり
reading: にあたって・にあたり
meanings: on the occasion of; at the time of (undertaking)
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋にあたって／にあたり
explanation: 〜にあたって・〜にあたり marks a significant moment — usually the start of an important undertaking — as the occasion for appropriate action. 開会にあたり = 'on the occasion of opening'. It is formal and forward-looking, used for milestones and ceremonies rather than everyday events. にあたって and にあたり are interchangeable, the latter a touch more formal.

synonyms.note: に際して is very close ('on the occasion of'); にあたって leans toward preparing to undertake something, 際して toward a special moment or event.
に先立ち means 'prior to / in advance of', stressing timing before the event; にあたって marks the occasion itself.

related.note: 上で is a more procedural 'in the course of / when doing'; にあたって singles out an important occasion.

meanings: because of that; for that reason (also: to that end)
explanation: そのため(に) refers back to something just stated and presents it as the reason for what follows — "because of that; for that reason." The に is optional. Depending on context it can also mean "to that end / for that purpose."

related.note: その結果 highlights the effect that followed; そのため(に) highlights the cause behind what follows.
そこで presents a deliberate action taken; そのため(に) presents the reason for the next statement.
ために is the general 'because of / in order to' pattern; そのため(に) packages a whole prior sentence as 'that.'

meanings: either ~ or ~ (for instance); ~ or ~ or something

meanings: in total contrast to ~; utterly unlike ~
structure: Noun［prior state, e.g. 昨日／普段］＋とは打って変わって

meanings: unless ~ (happens), it won't / can't ~
structure: Verb［ない form］＋ことには ～ない
explanation: 〜ないことには〜ない presents the first clause as an indispensable condition: unless that thing is done or comes about, the desirable result in the second clause is impossible. The main clause is always negative — nothing can move forward until the precondition is met. Common with 'try it and see' situations: 使ってみないことには = 'unless you actually try it'.

synonyms.note: てからでないと stresses sequence ('not until after ~'); ないことには frames the clause as a required condition for anything to happen.
ないと is the everyday 'unless / have to'; ないことには is more emphatic that nothing at all can start otherwise.

related.note: なければならない states a plain obligation to do something; ないことには says the result is unreachable without it.

meanings: somehow (or other); to (barely) manage to
explanation: どうにか means getting something done by some means or other, often only just barely — 'somehow, one way or another'. どうにか間に合った = somehow made it in time, どうにかしてほしい = I want it dealt with somehow. It can express relief at barely succeeding or a wish for some solution to a problem. It is close to なんとか in meaning and everyday register.

meanings: to receive; to get
structure: Noun［receiver］＋ は ＋ Noun［giver］＋ に／から ＋ Noun ＋ を ＋ もらう

meanings: far from; let alone; not to mention; on the contrary
structure: な-adjective［plain form］／い-adjective／Verb［plain form］＋ どころか
explanation: どころか denies one idea and replaces it with something further off. In one use, reality is the opposite of what was suggested — 謝るどころか、もっと怒り出した = far from apologizing, he got even angrier. In the other, it rules out a smaller thing to stress a bigger one — 漢字どころか、ひらがなも読めない = he can't read hiragana, let alone kanji. Either way, what comes after is more extreme.

synonyms.note: ばかりか adds a further, heavier point ('not only ... but even'); どころか can also flatly reverse the expectation.

related.note: むしろ says 'rather, if anything'; どころか denies the first idea outright and pushes to the opposite or beyond.

Before a noun, use に合った to describe something that suits or fits — 季節に合った服 ('clothes suited to the season').

synonyms.note: に応じて means 'in response to / depending on'; に合わせて stresses actively matching a target.

related.note: に沿って means 'along / in line with (a plan or guideline)'; に合わせて is tuning to fit.
に基づいて means 'based on (a foundation)'; に合わせて is adjusting to match.

meanings: suited to; suitable for; well-matched to (a group or purpose)
explanation: N向き says something happens to suit or is convenient for a certain group or purpose — 初心者向き = suited to beginners. It suggests a natural fit rather than deliberate design. 向き also literally means 'facing (a direction)', as in 南向き (south-facing).

related.note: 向け is deliberately made or aimed at a target; 向き is just a natural fit for that group.

meanings: bordering on; smacking of; having an (unfavourable) air of
explanation: 〜がましい is a suffix that turns a noun or verb stem into an い-adjective meaning 'coming across as ~, smacking of ~', always with a disapproving edge. It lives in a fixed set of formations: 言い訳がましい (sounding like an excuse), 押し付けがましい (pushy), 未練がましい (clinging), 差し出がましい (presumptuous). The word describes an unwelcome quality that a manner or attitude gives off.

synonyms.note: めく neutrally says something 'shows signs of / has a touch of'; がましい specifically adds an unfavourable, off-putting flavour.
っぽい is casual and can be neutral ('-ish, tends to'); がましい is formal and inherently critical.

meanings: the instant one saw / judged that ~
explanation: 〜と見るや is a literary, dramatic version of とみると: the very instant someone perceives or judges a situation, they immediately act — 'the moment he saw ~, he ...'. 隙ありと見るや、猫は飛びかかった = the instant it spotted an opening, the cat pounced. The や here marks that the action came without a beat's delay, not a question. It suits vivid narration.

synonyms.note: とみると shares the same core sense but is calmer and less dramatic than と見るや.
や否や also means 'the instant ~'; と見るや specifically pivots on the subject seeing or judging something first.

related.note: が早いか marks two actions almost overlapping in time; と見るや foregrounds the act of perceiving that triggers the response.
なり marks a second action right on the heels of the first; と見るや adds that a judgment of the situation set it off.

meanings: after piling ~ upon ~; through repeated ~
explanation: 〜に〜を重ねて repeats the same noun across に and を to stress that something was accumulated over and over: 努力に努力を重ねて = piling effort upon effort, 失敗に失敗を重ねる = heaping failure upon failure. It emphasizes the sheer repetition or layering of the same experience, usually as the drawn-out process leading to a hard-won result. The register is formal or written.

related.note: た末に marks the final outcome after a long process; 〜に〜を重ねて zooms in on the repeated piling-up of the same effort within such a process.

meanings: even when it has come to (this extreme point); even now that ~
explanation: 〜に至っても marks that even after a situation has reached an extreme or final stage, the expected change still fails to happen. It stresses that things have gone this far and yet — 締め切り当日に至っても = even when the very day of the deadline arrived. The main clause usually ends in a negative or in stubborn inaction. It is formal and built on 至る ('to reach').

related.note: に至る plainly states 'reaches (an extreme point)'; に至っても adds the concessive 'even having reached it, still ~'.
に至っては picks out the most extreme case to comment on; に至っても concedes that even at the extreme, nothing changed.

meanings: not something that ~ will settle; ~ing is not enough to resolve it
structure: Verb［て form］＋済むことではない
explanation: 〜て済むことではない declares that merely doing the stated action is not enough to put a matter to rest — the problem is too serious for that. 謝って済むことではない = this isn't something an apology will make right. 済む here means 'be settled / get by', so the negative says the issue won't be closed off just by that action, implying graver consequences or responsibility. It carries a reproachful, weighty tone.

synonyms.note: 〜では済まない says a situation won't end with just ~ (and worse will follow); て済むことではない specifically denies that a given action can settle the matter.
〜ずには済まない means one can't avoid doing ~ (it's unavoidable); て済むことではない means doing ~ isn't enough to resolve things — the opposite angle on 済む.

related.note: 〜て済む affirms that something can be gotten through or settled by ~; て済むことではない negates exactly that.

meanings: under; under the supervision / influence of
explanation: 〜の下で(もとで) means acting 'under' someone or something — under their guidance, authority, or a set of conditions. 有名な先生の下で学ぶ = study under a famous teacher; 厳しい規則の下で = under strict rules. Here 下 is read もと and means a governing influence or circumstance, not a physical 'below'. の下に is a close variant.

related.note: において marks a formal place or situation ('in / at'); の下で marks acting under a person's authority or a condition.
をもとに uses もと for a basis or source ('based on ~'); の下で means 'under the authority / conditions of'.

meanings: marks time, destination, or indirect target
isn't it (perhaps) that ~?; I rather think that ~
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ のではないだろうか
な-adjective／Noun ＋ なの ＋ ではないだろうか
explanation: 〜のではないだろうか is a soft, tentative way to put forward an opinion — literally 'isn't it perhaps that ~?', i.e. 'I rather think that ~.' It hedges a claim so it sounds considered rather than blunt: 彼は無理をしているのではないだろうか = I wonder if he isn't overdoing it. Common in essays and careful speech. のではないでしょうか is the polite form.

related.note: ではないか asserts or seeks agreement more directly; のではないだろうか is softer, voicing one's own tentative guess.
だろう states a plain conjecture 'probably'; のではないだろうか wraps that guess in a gentle rhetorical question.

meanings: at least; at the very least
explanation: 少なくとも means 'at least' — it states a guaranteed minimum, whether a quantity (少なくとも三千円はかかる = it will cost at least 3,000 yen) or a minimal claim you are sure of (少なくとも彼は嘘をつかない = at least he doesn't lie). It marks the floor below which things won't go.

synonyms.note: せめて expresses a wish for a bare minimum ('at least ~, if nothing else'); 少なくとも states a factual minimum.

related.note: 以上 marks '~ or more' as a suffix on a quantity; 少なくとも is an adverb setting the same lower bound.

meanings: in light of; in view of; against (a standard)
explanation: 〜に照らして takes an established standard — a law, rule, precedent, common sense, or past experience — and judges something against it. 法律に照らして = in light of the law, 判例に照らして = against precedent. It also appears as 〜に照らし合わせて ('cross-checking against'). This is formal, written Japanese used when weighing a case against a fixed criterion.

synonyms.note: に基づいて takes a source as the basis to act on; に照らして compares a case against a standard to evaluate it.
に沿って means 'keeping in line with (a policy/wish)'; に照らして means 'evaluated against (a criterion)'.

related.note: に則って means 'following (rules) as one acts'; に照らして means 'checking something against (a standard)'.

meanings: per; apiece; for each (unit)
explanation: 〜当たり attaches to a counter or unit noun to express a rate — 'per one of that unit'. 一箱当たり = per box, 一時間当たり = per hour. It is used when dividing a total across units, much like English 'per'. Here 当たり has nothing to do with 'hitting' or 'winning'; it is a fixed suffix meaning 'per'.

synonyms.note: につき also means 'per' in this rate sense; it additionally has a separate meaning 'due to', which 〜当たり never carries.

meanings: imperative form; blunt command 'do ~!'
structure: Verb（godan）［ー u → e］（書く → 書け）
Verb（ichidan）［る → ろ］（見る → 見ろ）
する → しろ ／ 来る → 来い
explanation: The 命令形 (imperative) is the plainest, most forceful way to order someone to do something — 'Do it!'. Godan verbs change their final -u to -e (書く → 書け, 待つ → 待て), ichidan verbs replace る with ろ (食べる → 食べろ), and the irregulars are しろ (する) and 来い (来る). It is strong and rough, used for orders, warnings, signs, and cheering.

antonyms.note: 〜な is the negative command ('don't do it'); the 命令形 is the positive command ('do it').

related.note: なさい is a firm but gentler order (parent to child, exam instructions); the imperative is rougher.
〜てください is the polite request, built on the て form — the courteous alternative to a bare command.

meanings: in; at; under (a particular situation, position, or era)
explanation: 〜にあって places the following statement within a special situation, position, or time — 'being in ~, situated in ~'. 非常時にあって = in a time of emergency, その立場にあって = holding that position. It sets up circumstances that are notable or extreme, and the main clause tells what holds true under them. The negative-conditional form にあっても means 'even in ~'. It is a formal, written expression.

synonyms.note: において neutrally marks a place, time, or field; にあって stresses being placed within a notable or trying situation.

related.note: とあって gives a special circumstance as the reason for what follows; にあって sets the circumstance as a backdrop without asserting cause.

meanings: to the very end; persistently; strictly / merely (nothing more than)
structure: あくまでも＋Verb／Sentence［persist to the end］
explanation: あくまでも has two linked uses. With a stance or effort it means 'thoroughly, to the bitter end, without giving way': あくまでも戦う = fight to the last, あくまでも自分の意見を通す = insist on one's view no matter what. Framing a statement, it means 'strictly / merely', limiting the claim: あくまでも個人的な意見 = purely a personal opinion, あくまでも一例 = just one example. In both, it stresses that the point holds firmly and without exception.

meanings: it's understandable that ~; no wonder ~

explanation: 〜のももっともだ means 'it's understandable / reasonable that ~' — given the situation, one can well see why someone feels or acts a certain way. ここまで待たされたら、彼が怒るのももっともだ = if he was kept waiting this long, it's understandable he got angry. もっとも here means 'reasonable, justified'. surface: ことこのうえない・このうえない
reading: ことこのうえない・このうえない
meanings: unsurpassed; in the extreme; couldn't be more ~
explanation: この上ない literally says 'there is nothing above this' — the degree is the highest possible. The tone is formal-written, and unlike 極まりない it works comfortably with positive qualities as well as negative ones.

related.note: の至り expresses an extreme of emotion in fixed formal phrases (光栄の至り); この上ない is a more general superlative.

surface: までだ・までのことだ
reading: までだ・までのことだ
meanings: merely; simply; that's all; nothing more than
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋までだ／までのことだ
Verb［た form］＋までだ／までのことだ
explanation: 〜までだ / 〜までのことだ plays an action down as nothing more than what is stated. After a dictionary-form verb it expresses calm resolve — 'if it comes to that, I'll simply ~' (だめなら、やり直すまでだ = if it fails, I'll just do it over). After a た-form verb it justifies — 'I merely ~, that's all' (事実を述べたまでだ = I only stated the facts, nothing more).

synonyms.note: のみ is a formal 'only'; までだ frames the action as the sole, modest recourse or as nothing more than stated.

related.note: までもない ('no need to go so far as') is a separate までも construction, not this 'merely ~' までだ.
だけ limits scope to 'only ~'; までだ adds the nuance of a modest, final recourse or a bare justification.

meanings: the reason is; this is because ~

explanation: なぜなら opens a sentence that gives the reason for something you just said. It typically pairs with から or のだ at the end — 'The reason is that ~'. You state a claim first, then a fresh sentence beginning なぜなら explains why. It belongs to writing and formal speech.

related.note: だって is the casual spoken 'because'; なぜなら is its formal, written counterpart.

meanings: to make something (into) ~
explanation: This pattern says someone deliberately changes a thing into a state. With nouns and な-adjectives, use にする (きれいにする = make it clean); with い-adjectives, swap い for く and add する (大きくする = make it bigger). related.note: にする also means 'decide on / choose'; here it means 'turn something into ~'.
